prompt: Which part of a cell controls the cell's activities and contains its genetic information?

options.text: Nucleus
Cell membrane
Cytoplasm
Vacuole

feedback.b: The cell membrane controls what goes in and out of the cell, not the cell's activities.
feedback.c: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance where many reactions happen.
feedback.d: The vacuole stores water and other substances.

hints: Think about where DNA is kept.
solution: The **nucleus** contains DNA, which carries the instructions that control the cell's activities.

prompt: Select **all** the structures found in plant cells but **not** in animal cells.

options.text: Cell wall
Chloroplast
Nucleus
Cell membrane
Large permanent vacuole

hints: Two of the options are found in every plant and animal cell.
Think about what a plant needs to do that an animal doesn't, such as photosynthesis and staying rigid.
solution: Plant cells have a **cell wall** (support), **chloroplasts** (photosynthesis) and a **large permanent vacuole** (stores water and keeps the cell firm). Both plant and animal cells have a nucleus and a cell membrane.

prompt: Match each cell part to its job.

right.text: Control what enters and leaves the cell

hints: Mitochondria are often called the cell's 'powerhouse'.
solution: Mitochondria → respiration; chloroplast → photosynthesis; cell membrane → controls what enters and leaves; cell wall → support.

prompt: Put these levels of organisation in order, from smallest to largest.
hints: A group of similar cells working together forms a tissue.
solution: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism. For example: muscle cell → muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system → human.

prompt: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece lens and a ×40 objective lens. What is the total magnification?
hints: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
solution: Total magnification $= 10 \times 40 = 400$, so the image is **×400**.

prompt: Name the green structures in a leaf cell where photosynthesis happens.
hints: They contain the green pigment chlorophyll.
solution: **Chloroplasts.** They contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

prompt: Animal cells have a cell [[a]] but no cell [[b]], so they do not have a fixed shape.
hints: One of these structures is rigid and found only in plants (and some other organisms).
solution: Animal cells have a cell **membrane** but no cell **wall**. The rigid cell wall is what gives plant cells their fixed shape.

prompt: Root cells of a plant do not contain chloroplasts, but leaf cells do. Explain why.
modelAnswer: Chloroplasts are where photosynthesis happens, and photosynthesis needs light. Leaf cells are exposed to sunlight, so they have chloroplasts to absorb light energy and make glucose. Root cells are underground where there is no light, so chloroplasts would be no use to them.

rubric.criterion: States that chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis
States that photosynthesis needs light (energy)
Links this to roots being underground with no light, so chloroplasts aren't needed

hints: What do chloroplasts do, and what do they need to do it?
solution: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, which needs light energy. Leaves receive light; roots grow in the dark soil, so chloroplasts would have no light to use.

prompt: What is the basic unit (building block) that all living things are made of?
hints: Every living thing, from bacteria to a kauri tree, is made of one or more of these.
solution: The **cell** is the basic unit of life. Some organisms, such as bacteria, are just one cell. Your body is made of trillions of cells.

prompt: Which part of a light microscope do you look through?

options.text: Eyepiece lens
Objective lens
Stage
Diaphragm

feedback.b: The objective lenses sit just above the slide. You look through the eyepiece at the top.
feedback.c: The stage is the flat platform that holds the slide.
feedback.d: The diaphragm controls how much light passes up through the slide.

hints: It's the lens at the top of the microscope, closest to your eye.
solution: You look through the **eyepiece lens**. It usually magnifies ×10, and it works together with the objective lens to magnify the specimen.

prompt: Which set of structures is found in a human cheek cell?

options.text: Nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and mitochondria
Nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and cell wall
Nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and chloroplasts
Cytoplasm, cell wall, large vacuole and chloroplasts

feedback.b: Cheek cells are animal cells, and animal cells have no cell wall.
feedback.c: Chloroplasts are only found in cells that photosynthesise, such as leaf cells. Cheek cells don't photosynthesise.
feedback.d: These are plant cell structures. A cheek cell has no cell wall, large vacuole or chloroplasts.

hints: A cheek cell is an animal cell.
Rule out any option that includes a structure found only in plant cells.
solution: A cheek cell is an animal cell, so it has a **nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and mitochondria**. It has no cell wall, no chloroplasts and no large permanent vacuole.

prompt:
A microscope gives a total magnification of ×600 when the ×40 objective lens is used. What is the magnification of the eyepiece lens?

Enter the number only (for example, 10 for ×10).
hints: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.
You know the total and the objective, so divide.
solution:
Eyepiece magnification $= 600 \div 40 = 15$, so the eyepiece is **×15**.

Check: $15 \times 40 = 600$ ✓

prompt: Put these steps for focusing a light microscope in the correct order.

items.text: Place the slide on the stage, with the lowest-power objective lens in position
Watching from the side, use the coarse focus to bring the lens close to the slide
Looking through the eyepiece, turn the coarse focus to move the lens and slide apart until the image appears
Use the fine focus to make the image sharp
Switch to a higher-power objective lens and refocus using only the fine focus

hints: Always start with the lowest-power objective lens.
Watch from the side while the lens moves towards the slide, so you don't crack the slide.
solution:
1. Slide on the stage, lowest-power objective in place.
2. Watching from the side, bring the lens close to the slide with the coarse focus.
3. Looking through the eyepiece, move the lens and slide apart with the coarse focus until the image appears.
4. Sharpen the image with the fine focus.
5. Change to a higher-power lens and use only the fine focus.

You only move the lens **away** from the slide while looking through the eyepiece, so you can't crash the lens into the slide.

prompt: Why do students add a drop of iodine solution to onion skin cells on a microscope slide?

options.text: To stain the cells so structures such as the nucleus are easier to see
To kill any bacteria that might be on the slide
To make the cells swell up so they are easier to see
To glue the cover slip firmly onto the slide

feedback.b: Killing bacteria isn't the reason. The stain is used to add colour and contrast.
feedback.c: The stain doesn't change the size of the cells. Magnification comes from the lenses.
feedback.d: The cover slip is held in place by the liquid underneath it, not by the stain.

hints: Onion skin cells are almost see-through.
solution: Onion cells are nearly transparent, so they are hard to see. Iodine is a **stain**: it colours parts of the cells, such as the nucleus and cell wall, so they show up clearly.

prompt: A plant cell wall is made of [[a]], which makes it strong. The large permanent vacuole is filled with [[b]], which pushes outwards and keeps the cell firm.
hints: The wall is made of a tough carbohydrate that also gives vegetables their fibre.
The liquid in the vacuole is a watery solution of sugars and salts.
solution: The cell wall is made of **cellulose**. The vacuole is filled with **cell sap**, a solution of water, sugars and salts. When the vacuole is full, it presses against the cell wall and keeps the cell firm.

prompt: Match each specialised cell to the feature that helps it do its job.

right.text: No nucleus, leaving more room to carry oxygen
Long, thin extension that gives a large surface area for absorbing water
A tail for swimming to the egg
Lots of mitochondria to release energy for movement

hints: Think about each cell's job first: carrying, absorbing, swimming, photosynthesising or moving.
solution: Red blood cell → no nucleus (more room for oxygen); root hair cell → long extension (large surface area); sperm cell → tail; palisade cell → many chloroplasts; muscle cell → many mitochondria (energy for contracting).

prompt: Hemi is looking at onion cells through the ×4 objective lens. He switches to the ×40 objective lens and refocuses. What will he notice?

options.text: The cells look bigger, but he can see fewer of them
The cells look smaller, and he can see more of them
The cells look the same size, but they are sharper
The cells look bigger, and he can see more of them

feedback.b: A higher-power lens magnifies more, so the cells look bigger, not smaller.
feedback.c: Changing to a higher-power lens increases magnification, so the cells look bigger.
feedback.d: When you zoom in, you see a smaller area of the slide, so fewer cells fit in the view.

hints: Think about zooming in on a photo on your phone.
What happens to how much of the picture you can see when you zoom in?
solution: The ×40 lens magnifies 10 times more than the ×4 lens, so each cell looks **bigger**. But the **field of view** (the area of the slide you can see) gets smaller, so **fewer cells** fit in the view. The image usually looks dimmer too.

prompt: A cell has a cell wall, a nucleus and a large permanent vacuole, but no chloroplasts. Which cell is it most likely to be?

options.text: A root hair cell from a plant
A cheek cell from a human
A palisade cell from a leaf
A red blood cell from a human

feedback.b: Cheek cells are animal cells, so they have no cell wall or large vacuole.
feedback.c: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
feedback.d: Red blood cells are animal cells with no cell wall. They also have no nucleus.

hints: The cell wall and large vacuole tell you it's a plant cell.
Which part of a plant gets no light?
solution: The cell wall and large vacuole show it is a **plant cell**. It has no chloroplasts, so it comes from a part of the plant that gets no light: a **root hair cell**.

prompt: Compare plant cells and animal cells. Give **two** similarities and **two** differences.
modelAnswer:
Similarities: both plant and animal cells have a nucleus, which contains DNA and controls the cell. Both have a cell membrane, which controls what enters and leaves the cell. (Both also have cytoplasm and mitochondria.)

Differences: plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose, but animal cells do not. Plant cells have chloroplasts for photosynthesis, but animal cells do not. Plant cells also have a large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, which animal cells do not have.

rubric.criterion: Gives one correct similarity (both have a nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm or mitochondria)
Gives a second, different correct similarity
Gives one correct difference (only plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts or a large permanent vacuole)
Gives a second, different correct difference

hints: List the structures found in both kinds of cell, then the ones found only in plant cells.
For a difference, say which cell has the structure and which doesn't.
solution:
| Structure | Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|---|
| Nucleus | ✓ | ✓ |
| Cell membrane | ✓ | ✓ |
| Cytoplasm | ✓ | ✓ |
| Mitochondria | ✓ | ✓ |
| Cell wall | ✓ | ✗ |
| Chloroplasts | ✓ (in green parts) | ✗ |
| Large permanent vacuole | ✓ | ✗ |

Any two shared structures are similarities. Any two plant-only structures are differences, as long as you say that animal cells don't have them.

prompt: A student's drawing of a plant cell is 50 mm long. The drawing has a magnification of ×250. What is the actual length of the cell in micrometres (µm)?
hints: Rearrange the formula: actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
Your first answer will be in millimetres. 1 mm = 1000 µm.
solution:
Actual size = image size ÷ magnification $= 50 \div 250 = 0.2$ mm.

Convert to micrometres: $0.2 \times 1000 = 200$ µm.

The cell is **200 µm** long.

prompt: In Aroha's photo, a cheek cell is 40 mm wide. She knows the real cell is 80 µm wide. She works out 40 ÷ 80 = 0.5 and writes "magnification ×0.5". What went wrong?

options.text: She didn't put both sizes in the same units. 40 mm = 40 000 µm, so the magnification is ×500.
She divided the wrong way round. It should be 80 ÷ 40, so the magnification is ×2.
She should have multiplied the two sizes, so the magnification is ×3200.
Nothing went wrong. A magnification below ×1 is normal for photos of cells.

feedback.b: The formula is image size ÷ actual size, so she divided the right way round. Her mistake was mixing mm and µm.
feedback.c: Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. You never multiply the two sizes.
feedback.d: A magnification below ×1 would mean the photo is smaller than the real cell. A 40 mm photo of a tiny cell must be magnified a lot.

hints: Look at the units of each measurement.
solution: Both sizes must be in the same units. $40 \text{ mm} = 40\,000\ \mu\text{m}$, so the magnification $= 40\,000 \div 80 = 500$. The photo is magnified **×500**.

prompt: Name the flat part of a microscope that the slide sits on.
hints: It usually has two clips to hold the slide in place.
solution: The slide sits on the **stage**, held in place by clips. Light shines up through a hole in the stage.

prompt: Which part of a cell releases energy from glucose by respiration?

options.text: Mitochondria
Chloroplasts
Nucleus
Cell wall

feedback.b: Chloroplasts **store** energy in glucose by photosynthesis. Mitochondria release that energy.
feedback.c: The nucleus contains DNA and controls the cell.
feedback.d: The cell wall supports and protects a plant cell.

hints: They are often called the cell's 'powerhouses'.
solution: **Mitochondria** carry out respiration, which releases energy from glucose. Both plant cells and animal cells have mitochondria.

prompt: What is the jelly-like substance that fills a cell, where many of the cell's chemical reactions happen?
hints: It surrounds the nucleus and fills the space inside the cell membrane.
solution: **Cytoplasm** is a jelly-like substance made mostly of water. Many chemical reactions happen in it, and the other parts of the cell sit in it.

prompt: Which unit is most often used to measure the size of cells?

options.text: Micrometres (µm)
Centimetres (cm)
Kilograms (kg)
Millilitres (mL)

feedback.b: Most cells are far smaller than 1 cm. A typical cheek cell is about 0.006 cm across, so centimetres are too big to be useful.

hints: Cells are tiny. You need a unit much smaller than a millimetre.
solution: Cells are usually measured in **micrometres (µm)**. 1 mm = 1000 µm. A human cheek cell is about 60 µm across, and a red blood cell is about 8 µm.

prompt: Select **all** the structures found in **both** plant cells and animal cells.

options.text: Nucleus
Cell membrane
Cytoplasm
Mitochondria
Cell wall
Chloroplasts
Large permanent vacuole

hints: Think about which structures every living cell needs, whether it photosynthesises or not.
Do plant cells need to release energy from food?
solution:
**Both:** nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm and mitochondria. Plant cells respire too, so they need mitochondria.

**Plant cells only:** cell wall, chloroplasts (in green parts) and a large permanent vacuole.

hints: To change millimetres into micrometres, multiply by 1000.

prompt: Match each part of a light microscope to its job.

right.text: The lens just above the slide; swap it to change the magnification
The flat platform that holds the slide
Moves the stage (or lens) a long way, to find the image quickly
Makes small changes to sharpen the image
Controls how much light passes through the slide

hints: There are two lenses: one near your eye and one near the slide.
The two focus knobs differ in how far they move the lens.
solution:
- Eyepiece lens: the lens you look through
- Objective lens: the lens just above the slide (swap it to change magnification)
- Stage: holds the slide
- Coarse focus: big movements, to find the image
- Fine focus: small movements, to sharpen the image
- Diaphragm: controls the amount of light

options.text: It is very thin and pressed tightly against the inside of the cell wall
Plant cells have a cell wall instead of a cell membrane
It is on the outside of the cell wall, so it was cut off the slide
The iodine stain dissolves the cell membrane, so it disappears

feedback.b: Plant cells have **both**. The wall gives support; the membrane, just inside it, controls what goes in and out.
feedback.c: The cell membrane is **inside** the cell wall, not outside it.
feedback.d: Iodine stains parts of the cell. It doesn't dissolve the membrane.

hints: Plant cells have both a cell wall and a cell membrane.
Where is the membrane, compared with the wall?

prompt: In Mele's drawing, the labelled cell is drawn 60 mm long. The real cell is 300 µm long. Calculate the magnification of her drawing.
hints: Both lengths must be in the same units first. 1 mm = 1000 µm.
Magnification = image size ÷ actual size.
solution:
Convert the drawing length into micrometres: $60 \text{ mm} = 60 \times 1000 = 60\,000$ µm.

Magnification $= 60\,000 \div 300 = 200$, so the drawing is **×200**.

prompt: When you make a slide, you lower the cover slip onto the drop of liquid slowly, at an angle, using a mounted needle. Why?

options.text: To stop air bubbles getting trapped under the cover slip
To spread the stain evenly across all of the cells
To stop the objective lens touching the specimen
To stop the specimen drying out during the lesson

feedback.b: The stain spreads through the liquid by itself. Lowering the cover slip at an angle is about pushing air out.
feedback.c: The cover slip does protect the lens and the specimen, but lowering it at an angle is for a different reason.
feedback.d: A cover slip does slow down drying, but that doesn't depend on lowering it at an angle.

hints: Think about what could get trapped between the cover slip and the liquid.
solution: Lowering the cover slip slowly at an angle pushes the air out ahead of the liquid, so **air bubbles** don't get trapped. Under the microscope, air bubbles look like circles with thick black edges, and they can hide the cells.

prompt: A light microscope makes the image upside down and back to front. Ana sees a cell near the **right-hand** edge of her view. Which way should she move the slide to bring the cell to the centre?

options.text: To the right
To the left
Away from her
Towards her

feedback.b: Because the image is reversed, moving the slide left makes the image move right, further from the centre.
feedback.c: Moving the slide away from or towards her moves the image up or down, not across to the centre.
feedback.d: Moving the slide away from or towards her moves the image up or down, not across to the centre.

hints: The image is reversed, so it moves the opposite way to the slide.
She needs the image to move left.
solution:
The image is reversed, so moving the slide one way makes the image move the **opposite** way. Moving the slide **to the right** makes the image move left, towards the centre.

A handy rule: move the slide towards the side where the cell appears.

prompt: Photosynthesis happens in the [[a]], which use light energy to make glucose. Respiration happens in the [[b]], which release energy from glucose. A palisade cell in a leaf contains [[c]].
hints: Does a leaf cell need to release energy from glucose, as well as make glucose?
solution: Photosynthesis happens in **chloroplasts**; respiration happens in **mitochondria**. Palisade cells photosynthesise **and** respire, so they contain **both**.

prompt: Tama has a microscope with a ×10 eyepiece lens and three objective lenses: ×4, ×10 and ×40. Describe how to work out the total magnification, and explain why he should **start** with the ×4 objective lens.
modelAnswer: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification. With the ×4 objective it is 10 × 4 = ×40 (and ×100 and ×400 with the other two lenses). He should start with the ×4 lens because it shows the widest field of view, so it is much easier to find the specimen and focus on it. The low-power lens is also shorter, so there is more space between it and the slide, and less chance of cracking the slide.

rubric.criterion: States that total magnification = eyepiece × objective (e.g. 10 × 4 = ×40)
Explains that the lowest power gives the widest field of view, so the specimen is easier to find and focus (or there is less risk of hitting the slide)

hints: How do the two lenses combine?
What happens to how much of the slide you can see as you zoom in?
solution: Multiply the two lens magnifications: $10 \times 4 = 40$, so the lowest setting is ×40. Starting at low power gives the **widest field of view**, so you can find the specimen easily, then zoom in on the part you want.

prompt: Which of these is a rule for making a good scientific drawing of cells?

options.text: Use clear, single pencil lines, no shading, and ruled label lines
Colour in each part, so it is easy to tell the parts apart
Draw every single cell that you can see in the field of view
Use a pen instead of a pencil, so the lines don't smudge

feedback.b: Scientific drawings aren't coloured or shaded. Clear outlines and labels show the parts.
feedback.c: You only need to draw a few cells, accurately and large enough to label clearly.
feedback.d: Use a sharp pencil, so you can rub out and fix mistakes.

hints: Scientific drawings are about clear, accurate outlines, not making them look pretty.
solution: A scientific drawing uses a **sharp pencil**, clear single lines, **no shading or colour**, a title, the magnification, and label lines drawn with a ruler that do not cross each other.

prompt: Mele's estimate of the cell length may not be very accurate. Explain **two** reasons why, and suggest how she could get a better estimate.
modelAnswer: The cells aren't all the same size, so the eight cells she counted might be bigger or smaller than average. She only counted along one line, in one part of the slide. The ruler only has millimetre marks, so 1.6 mm is itself an estimate, and real cells rarely line up perfectly end to end. To get a better estimate, she should count the cells along several different lines and in different parts of the slide, work out the cell length each time, and calculate the mean.

rubric.criterion: Gives one valid reason (e.g. cells vary in size; she counted along only one line; 1.6 mm is hard to measure exactly with a millimetre ruler; cells don't line up perfectly)

solution: Sources of error include **cells varying in size**, **counting along only one line**, and **measuring the field of view** with a millimetre ruler. Repeating the count in several places and taking the **mean** gives a more reliable estimate.

prompt: An amoeba is a single-celled organism. A human is made of trillions of cells. Explain why a human needs specialised cells organised into tissues, organs and systems, but an amoeba does not.
modelAnswer: In an amoeba, the one cell has to carry out every life process itself: it feeds, respires, gets rid of waste, senses and moves. That works because it is tiny. A human is far too big for one kind of cell to do everything, so cells are specialised for particular jobs: for example, red blood cells carry oxygen, muscle cells contract and nerve cells carry messages. Similar specialised cells are grouped into tissues, tissues into organs, and organs into systems, so each job is done well and all the parts work together to keep the whole body alive.

rubric.criterion: States that the single cell of an amoeba carries out all the life processes by itself
Explains that human cells are specialised for different jobs, with an example (e.g. red blood cells carry oxygen; muscle cells contract)
Explains that specialised cells are organised into tissues, organs and systems that work together, so each job is done well for the whole body

hints: Which life processes does the single cell of an amoeba have to carry out?
Give an example of a human cell that does one special job.
solution: One cell can do everything only when the organism is tiny. In a large organism, cells **specialise** (division of labour). Groups of specialised cells form **tissues**, tissues form **organs**, and organs form **systems**, which work together to keep the organism alive.

prompt: Kiri says, "Plant cells need a cell wall and a large vacuole, but animal cells can manage without them." Explain why she is right.
modelAnswer: A plant has no skeleton. Its cell walls are strong and rigid, and when the large vacuole is full of water it pushes outwards against the wall, keeping each cell firm. Lots of firm cells pressing together hold the plant upright, so its leaves can reach the light. The wall also stops the cell bursting when it takes in water. Animals are supported by a skeleton instead (bones, or an exoskeleton in insects), and many animal cells, such as muscle cells, need to be flexible so they can change shape and move. A rigid wall would get in the way.

rubric.criterion: States that the cell wall is strong and rigid, giving support or stopping the cell bursting
Explains that a full vacuole pushes against the wall to keep cells firm, which holds the plant upright (plants have no skeleton)
Explains that animals are supported by a skeleton, and many animal cells need to be flexible to move or change shape

hints: How does a plant stay upright without bones?
What supports an animal, and why might its cells need to change shape?
solution: Plants rely on **firm cells** for support: the rigid **cell wall** plus a **full vacuole** pushing against it. Animals have a **skeleton** for support, and their cells often need to be flexible, so they have only a cell membrane.

Cell P, which is about 1.3 times as long as cell Q
Cell Q, which is 4 times as long as cell P
Cell P, which is 3 times as long as cell Q

feedback.b: You compared the drawings, but they are at different magnifications. Work out each real length first.
feedback.c: You compared only the magnifications. You need to use the drawing lengths as well.
feedback.d: Check your working: real length = drawing length ÷ magnification. Cell P is 0.1 mm long and cell Q is 0.3 mm long.

Then compare the two real sizes.
solution:
Cell P: $40 \div 400 = 0.1$ mm. Cell Q: $30 \div 100 = 0.3$ mm.

$0.3 \div 0.1 = 3$, so **cell Q is really 3 times as long** as cell P, even though its drawing is shorter.

prompt: Mature human red blood cells have no nucleus and no mitochondria. Explain **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of this for the red blood cell.
modelAnswer:
Advantage: without a nucleus there is more room inside the cell for haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen. Without mitochondria, the cell doesn't use up any of the oxygen it is carrying. Both mean more oxygen is delivered to the body's cells for respiration.

Disadvantage: with no nucleus, the cell has no DNA, so it can't make new proteins to repair itself, and it can't divide. Red blood cells only last about four months, so the bone marrow has to make millions of new ones every second.

rubric.criterion: Gives an advantage: more room for haemoglobin, or the cell doesn't use up the oxygen it carries
Explains why this matters: more oxygen is delivered to the body's cells for respiration
Gives a disadvantage: with no nucleus (DNA) it can't repair itself or divide, so it doesn't live long and must be replaced

hints: What is a red blood cell's job, and what could fill the space a nucleus would take up?
What does the nucleus normally let a cell do?
solution: Losing the nucleus and mitochondria helps the cell **carry and deliver more oxygen**. The cost is that it has no DNA, so it **cannot repair itself or divide** and only lives for about four months.
